asked questions (FAQs) . 
 Submit all questions to the Grants Administration Unit at archgrants@nysed.gov. Questions and 
their answers will be posted to the New York State Archives’ LGRMIF FAQ webpage , which 
will be updated as needed.  LGRMIF applicants requesting in excess of $25,000 are required to comply with SED’s Minority and Women- Owned Business Enterprises (M/WBE) policy. Compliance can be achieved by one 
of the following methods: full participation, partial participation (partial  request for a waiver), or 
no participation (full request for a waiver). Full participation by meeting or exceeding the M/WBE participation goal for this grant is the preferred method. Additional information is contained under the Procurement section.  
  

8 
 Application Reminders  
 
• The State Archives will award grants based on funding available for the 2026- 2027 
Local Government Records Management Improvement Fund grant year. As required 
by law, $1,000,000 will be allocated from available funds for projects for the City of New York.  
 
• The deadline for requesting a new  eGrants user account has been increased to 10 
business days prior to the posted application deadline. If your local government’s RMO had an eGrants account but they no longer hold that position, a new  account 
needs to be created for the current RMO and is subject to the deadline specified above . The Grants Administration Unit cannot make exceptions to this closing date. 
 
• The Institutional Authorization form no longer requires a signature from your records management officer (RMO). Only an original signature from your CEO/CAO is required.  
 
• The State Archives strongly encourages all applicants to verify that the information in SED’s client database, SEDREF, is correct by accessing the SEDREF public portal . 
This information is  about your local government, which will populate the application 
form. If it is incorrect, submit a revised Standard Data Capture Form  (SDCF) no later 
than two weeks prior to submitting your application so we can update your SEDREF 
record. The revised SDCF can be emailed to archgrants@nysed.gov. If the 
information in SEDREF is correct, there is no need to submit an SDCF with your application. 
 
• The Payee Information form is no longer required to be submitted with an application. If the Grants Administration Unit (GAU) needs the form from your institution, the GAU will contact you. If your institution does not have a vendor ID, however, you will s till need to submit the form with the NYSED Substitute W -9. 
 
  

9 
 Timetable  
 
26 February 2026  Questions that have not already been addressed in this guide or through 
the frequently asked questions (FAQs) must be submitted to 
archgrants@nysed.gov  before 5:00 pm on this date.  
18 March  2026  Due date for submitting a Notice of Intent (NOI) to apply for an 
LGRMIF grant for the 2026- 2027 grant year. Note: This applies only to 
not-for-profit volunteer fire companies and volunteer ambulance 
services.  
18 March  2026  Registration forms requesting new eGrants user accounts must be 
submitted before 5:00 pm on this date.  *If a former RMO had an 
account, it is not transferable  to the current RMO. Please check with the 
Grants Administration Unit prior to the deadline if you are not sure about 
your RMO’s account status . 
18 March  2026  Standard Data Capture Forms to update applicants’ information in 
SEDREF and the application sheet in eGrants must be submitted before 
5:00 pm on this date. Applicants are strongly encouraged to verify that the information in SED’s client database, SEDREF, is correct by 
accessing the SEDREF public portal.  
1 April  2026  Grant applications must be submitted electronically before 5:00 pm on 
this date. Also, the paper signature forms required for all applications 
must be postmarked by this date.  
1 July 2026  Earliest date grants projects may start, contingent on final approval from 
the Division of the Budget and the Office of the State Comptroller.  
1 June 2027  All budget amendment templates must be submitted electronically before 
5:00 pm on this date. Also, the paper FS -10-A form, Proposed 
Amendment, if required, must be postmarked by this date.  
30 June 2027  All work on grants projects must be completed.  
31 July 2027  Final Reports must be submitted electronically and form FS -10-F, Final 
Expenditure Report, must be postmarked by this date.  
Note:  Grant recipients who have not submitted the necessary M/WBE forms 
during the application process should submit them electronically within thirty days from the date of notice of grant award. Failure to do so may 
result in loss of funding.  
   

10 
 Eligibility Requirements  
 
To be eligible to apply for an LGRMIF grant, most local governments in New York State are required to have the following in place by the application deadline:  
 
• Records Management Officer (RMO) appointed  
• Adopt the State Archives’ Retention and Disposition Schedule for New York Local 
Government Records (LGS -1)  
 
The only exceptions to this are the City of New York and its five county clerks and five district attorneys, community school districts in New York City, and housing authorities, none of which are required to have RMOs or to adopt the State Archives records retention and disposition schedule. Please note that although NYC agencies are not required to have RMOs appointed for the LGRMIF program, they are required to have an RMO under the Charter/rules of the City.  The State Education Department’s (SED’s) Grants Finance Unit will not release grant funds if you have failed to file the required final fiscal or narrative reports for any SED grant (which includes LGRMIF grants). Please also note that an application will not be forwarded for review if you have not submitted all final reports associated with previously awarded grants, exclusive of the current grant award period. 
Local Authorities  
 In the past, the State Archives considered Public Benefit Corporations with local or regional jurisdiction to be independent units of local government and therefore eligible to apply for LGRMIF funding. Currently, the State Archives considers local Authori ties under the Public 
Authorities Law , including public benefit corporations, to be local governments and eligible to 
apply for LGRMIF funding. The State Archives considers state authorities under the Public Authorities Law to be state agencies and not eligible for LGRMIF funding. However, st ate 
authorities previously considered by the State Archives to be local governments and who previously received LGRMIF funding may continue to apply for LGRMIF funding as the State Archives transitions their status from local government to state agency and develops the 
necessary records retention and disposition schedule. 
Community Colleges  
 A community college sponsored by more than one county may apply for and receive grant payment as a separate local government. A community college sponsored by a single county may apply for grant funding only through its county’s RMO and with the approval of the county’s chief administrative official, whose signature is required on the appropriate required paper forms. All pertinent applicant information will refer to the county only, not the community college, with the exception of naming a project director . 
 A single county may apply for an additional grant so long as that application focuses entirely on the records of its community college. In both cases grant payment will be made to the county as 

11 
 the eligible entity.  
Fire Districts, Volunteer Fire Companies, Emergency Rescue 
Services, and Ambulance Services  
 
Fire districts are eligible to apply for LGRMIF grants because they are local governments, but they must meet the above eligibility requirements.  Pursuant to Chapter 508 of the Laws of 2014, volunteer fire companies and voluntary ambulance services are eligible to apply for LGRMIF grants. As they are not -for-profit entities, not local 
governments under the Local Government Records Law, they are not subject to the above eligibility requirements.  
 Not-for-profit entities other than volunteer fire companies incorporated under section 1402 of the 
Not-For-Profit Corporation Law are required to register in the New York Statewide Financial 
System (SFS) , and to complete the Vendor Prequalification process in order for their LGRMIF 
grant applications to be evaluated. Additional information on the prequalification process is available below and at the end of this document.  
 Emergency rescue services are neither local governments under the Local Government Records Law, nor covered by Chapter 508 of the Laws of 2014. Consequently, they are not eligible to apply for LGRMIF grants. 
Libraries  
 Public libraries that are independent local government entities or units of other local governments are eligible to apply for funding. Libraries that are a unit of another local government would have to apply through their respective governing body. For additional information, please consult the State Archives’ publication “ Retention and Disposition of Library 
and Library System Records ”.  
Charter Schools  
 Charter schools are not local governments under the Local Government Records Law and are not subject to the State Archives records disposition authority. As a result, they are not eligible to apply for LGRMIF funding.  Please contact the State Archives Grants Administration Unit at archgrants@nysed.gov for all 
questions about LGRMIF grant application eligibility.  
  

12 
 NYC Department of Records and Information Services (DORIS) Grants  
 
By law, the City of New York can receive up to $1 million in LGRMIF grant funds each year. The departments of New York City apply through the standard application process and must compete for funding, just as other applicants. As part of this $1 million al lowance, DORIS, 
which directly administers LGRMIF grants to New York City departments, is also eligible for a grant of up to $200,000 to support the administration of these grants and may also apply for a grant to address its own archives and records management issues.  
 For the purposes of LGRMIF grants, individual agencies of the City of New York are treated as local governments. Agencies may apply for individual grants focused solely on their respective agencies and may request up to $75,000. Alternatively, two or more agencies may band together to apply for a shared services application. In which case, the money for such grant projects will be part of the $1,000,000 allowance to New York City.  
 DORIS, as the administrator of LGRMIF grants to the City of New York, shall provide the State Archives with a listing of projects proposed by New York City departments in priority order, including the amount requested for each project. This listing should be part of the cover letter that accompanies the signed FS -10 budgets that are submitted in hard copy to the Grants 
Administration Unit. In the event of a tie where there is not enough money to fund all tying projects, the application or applications that will be funded are those that are the higher priority without exceeding the amount available.  
NYC Board of Education 
 The New York City Board of Education may now apply for an LGRMIF grant independent of NYC DORIS. The department must meet eligibility requirements and its RMO must have a State Archives eGrants user account. 
Prequalification Requirements  
 The State of New York has implemented a statewide prequalification process  designed to 
facilitate prompt contracting for not -for-profit vendors. This does not apply to local 
governments.   All not -for-profit vendors are required to pre -qualify prior to grant application. This includes all 
currently funded not -for-profit institutions that have already received an award and are in the 
middle of the program cycle . Proposals received from  nonprofit applicants that are not 
Prequalified in the Statewide Financial System (SFS) by 5:00 PM on the proposal due date of April 1, 2026 cannot be evaluated. Such proposals will be disqualified from further consideration. Please see the “Prequalification for Individual Applications” section for additional 
information.  Note:  Volunteer Firefighter Companies incorporated under §1402 of the Not -For-Profit 
Corporation Law are no longer required to pre -qualify in order to be eligible to apply for 
LGRMIF grants. 

13 
 Notice of Intent  
 
The Notice of Intent (NOI) is not a requirement for submitting a complete application by the application date ; however, NYSED encourages all prospective applicants to submit an NOI to 
ensure a timely and thorough review and rating process. A non- profit applicant’s NOI will also 
help to facilitate timely review of their prequalification materials. The notice of intent is a simple email notice stating your organization’s (use the legal name) intent to submit an application for this grant. Please also include your organization’s NYS Vendor ID. The due date is March 18, 
2026 at 5:00 PM. Please send the NOI to the State Archives, Grants Administration Unit, at archgrants@nysed.gov.  
  

14 
 Types of Grants  
Introduction  
 
Two types of competitive grants are available: Shared Services and Individual. Each type has multiple project categories: Disaster Management, Inactive Records, Historical Records, Files Management, and Document Conversion and Access. An overview of these categories, including category requirements and eligible activities, follows later in this document.  Applicants may submit or be a party to only one grant application, unless the second application is for a project under the Disaster Management category or in the case of a county where the second application is focused entirely on the records of its community college. The maximum amount allowed for a Disaster Management project is $10,000 when an applicant applies for this as a second application. If an applicant is submitting only one application and that application is for Disaster Management, the applic ant may request up to $75,000 (for an Individual project) or  
$150,000 (for a Shared Services project). No local government can be a party to three or more competitive grant applications in the same year under any circumstances.  
 
Shared Services Grants  
 Shared Services Grants involve two or more local governments working together, with one government acting as the lead. Shared Services projects continue to be a priority for funding at the State Archives.  
 Applicants proposing a Shared Services project may request up to $150,000. To be eligible for funding, a Shared Services application must demonstrate how the grant project will establish an ongoing cooperative relationship between governments that results in sustainable programmatic change. Note that the New York State General Municipal Law Section 119- O states that 
municipal corporations and districts have the power to enter into agreements, including shared services agreements, with each other but that the maximum term of such agreements cannot exceed five years, unless another law otherwise provides for a longer term.  
 Applicants for Shared Services grants must address each of the following:  
 
• Prove there is need for the project. If a needs assessment is essential for proving the viability of a project, it is the responsibility of the governments involved to ensure a needs assessment is submitted with the application. 
• Demonstrate the clear financial and administrative advantages of working together by including a cost -benefit analysis that demonstrates the cost savings of implementing 
the proposed project. 
• Any local government that is integral to the success or sustainability of a Shared Services project must be listed either as the lead applicant or a participating partner.  
• Demonstrate the mutual benefits of the project to all participants.  
• Provide information on the type, size, and function of the governments and government departments involved, detailed information about the records that will be 

15 
 the focus of the project, and the basis of all costs. 
• Include a signed Shared Services Agreement Form for each participating institution 
of your project. Scan the signed form(s) and upload the form(s) to your application as 
an attachment. Please use "SS Agreement" as the description for your attachment. If a 
participating institution is not listed in eGrants, have the institution complete and 
submit a Standard Data Capture Form  to archgrants@nysed.gov.  
• Demonstrate the full participation and support of all participants. Note that this 
participation and support cannot be fulfilled merely by submitting the required Shared Services agreement forms, which only address the willingness of a local government to participate in a Shared Services grant project. Each Shared Services application must include information about how the participants will continue to work together into the future.  
• Demonstrate that the proposed project will result in ongoing, positive programmatic change involving an alliance of two or more local governments. Also, demonstrate that all participating local governments are committed to supporting and expanding project results, through dedicated funds and staff, for the long term.  
 All of the following administrative requirements must also be met by Shared Services applicants:  
 
• One of the local government participants must be designated to serve as the lead applicant and fiscal agent for the grant. The lead applicant and participating local government partners must be eligible grant recipients, as defined by the program statute o r regulation.  
• The lead applicant must be responsible for the greatest percentage of the budget relative to the other collaborating members.  
• In the event a grant is awarded for a Shared Services project, the award will be prepared in the name of the lead applicant only. 
 The lead applicant must meet the following requirements:  
 
• Must be an eligible grant recipient as defined by statute. 
• Must receive and administer the grant funds and submit the required reports to account for the use of grant funds. 
• Must require local government partners to provide a letter of intent. Each letter must explain what the government will do in the course of the project; how funds, personnel, facilities, and tasks will be shared; and what benefits will be gained. Each letter must be signed by the chief administrative officer of the participating government.  
• Must be an active member of the partnership.  
• Cannot act as a flow -through for grant funds to pass to other recipients.  
• Is prohibited from sub- granting funds to other recipients, but the lead applicant is 
permitted to contract for services with other partners or consultants to provide services that the lead applicant cannot provide itself. 
• Must be responsible for the performance of any services provided by the partners, consultants, or other organizations and must coordinate how each will participate.

grants.title: 2026 Title I, Section 1003 School Improvement Grant (SIG) – Planning
grants.summary: Funds planning and development of district and school improvement plans for eligible districts and schools under the Elementary and Secondary Education Act (ESEA).
grants.description: The 2026 Title I, Section 1003 School Improvement Grant (SIG) – Planning provides funding to support the development and implementation of district and school continuous improvement plans as required under the Elementary and Secondary Education Act (ESEA). Eligible districts and schools include newly identified Target Districts and schools identified for Comprehensive Support and Improvement (CSI), Additional Targeted Support and Improvement (ATSI), and Targeted Support and Improvement (TSI). Applications must be submitted through the NYSED Business Portal, and funds can be used for staff participation, parent/family involvement, travel to NYSED Regional Training, and BOCES Needs Assessment and Planning Support.
grants.eligibility_notes: Eligible districts include newly identified Target Districts and schools identified for CSI, ATSI, or TSI. Charter schools and districts with only schools identified for Local Support and Improvement (LSI) are not eligible.
eligible_applicant_types: Schools identified for CSI, ATSI, or TSI
key_requirements: Must be a newly identified Target District or school identified for CSI, ATSI, or TSI.
Application must be submitted through the NYSED Business Portal.
Funds must be used for eligible activities such as needs assessment, planning, and training.
Signed PDF and FS-10 budget form must be submitted.
No carryover of funds; all costs must be encumbered during the project period.

2026 Title I, Section 1003 School Improvement Grant (SIG) – Planning
Grant Announcement/Instructions
2026 Title I, Section 1003 School Improvement Grant – Planning (PDF Version)
2026 Title I, Section 1003 School Improvement Grant – Planning (Word Version)
Full RFP
The online application is available to the assigned local education agency (LEA) through the
NYSED Business Portal
.   Select the survey titled “2026 Title I, 1003 School Improvement Grant (Planning).”
Purpose of 2026 Title I, 1003 SIG (Planning) Funds
Section 1003 of the Elementary and Secondary Education Act (ESEA) requires that State Education Agencies allocate funds to the assigned LEA for Target District support and schools identified for Comprehensive Support and Improvement (CSI), Additional Targeted Support and Improvement (ATSI), and Targeted Support and Improvement (TSI) to support the development and implementation of their individual district and school continuous improvement plans.  The 2026 Title I, 1003 School Improvement Grant (SIG) Planning funds are provided to support the planning and development of the 2026–27 district and school improvement plans as required under the ESEA.
Eligibility
District-Level Improvement Plan Development
The following districts are eligible for 2026 Title I, 1003 SIG (Planning) funding to support the development of the district-level improvement plan:
Newly Identified Target Districts
The following districts are
not
eligible for 2026 Title I, 1003 SIG (Planning) funding to support the development of the district-level improvement plan:
Previously Identified Target Districts*
School-Level Improvement Plan Development
Districts with the following schools are eligible for 2026 Title I, 1003 SIG (Planning) funding to support the development of a school-level plan(s):
Schools previously identified for Local Support and Improvement (LSI) that are now identified for Comprehensive Support and Improvement.
Districts with the following schools are
not
eligible for 2026 Title I, 1003 SIG (Planning) funding to support the development of school-level plans:
Districts that only have schools identified for LSI
Schools identified for LSI
Schools identified for CSI, ATSI, or TSI last year that remain identified*
Charter schools
*Re-Identified Target Districts, and Schools that began the 2025–26 SY in the TSI, ATSI or CSI support model and remain identified should access the 2025-26 Title I, 1003 SIG (Basic) funding to support the development of their 2026–27 improvement plans.
See Attachment I for a list of eligible Target Districts and 2026 Title I, 1003 SIG (Planning) funding allocations.  The individual support model for districts and schools can be found online at:
https://data.nysed.gov/
.
Funding
Eligible districts will receive the following allocations for 2026 Title I, 1003 SIG (Planning) funds:
Newly Identified Target District - $20,000 per district
Target Districts with a school(s) previously identified for LSI that are now identified for CSI - $20,000 per school
Allowable Uses of Funds
Districts may use 2026 Title I, 1003 SIG (Planning) funds for the following activities:
CATEGORY 1:
Staff participation in the completion of NYSED needs assessment activities and the development of the 2026-27 district-level and/or school-level improvement plan(s).
CATEGORY 2:
Support for parent/family participation in the development of the 2026-27 district-level and/or school-level improvement plan(s).
CATEGORY 3:
(For School Plan Development Only) Travel to NYSED Regional Training.
CATEGORY 4:
BOCES Needs Assessment and Planning Support. **
**If the BOCES does not provide Needs Assessment and Planning Support and an LEA would like to use any amount over $9,500 of 2026 Title I, 1003 SIG (Planning) funds, please contact
fieldsupport@nysed.gov
so that we can provide guidance on the rigorous review process that must be used to identify and evaluate any third-party vendor receiving funds through this grant.
Title I, 1003 SIG funds cannot be used to purchase any office equipment and/or furniture, general office supplies, and/or food/light refreshments for staff meetings within the district.  If the LEA wishes to fund an expense that would support schools in the CSI, ATSI, or TSI support models, SIG Basic funds could only be used for the portion that will go toward eligible schools.  Any support for non-eligible schools must be covered by a different funding source.
Project Period
January 1, 2026 to July 31, 2026
Application Deadline
Completed applications are due by
February 27, 2026
, and will be reviewed on a rolling basis. LEAs are encouraged to submit as soon as possible to expedite the review and approval process of 2026 Title I, 1003 SIG (Planning) funds.
LEAs must complete all sections of the online application and are required to answer questions marked with a red asterisk. If a required question has not been completed, the business portal will highlight it in red and the section of the application will be flagged. The applicant will be unable to submit the application to NYSED for final review if a required question remains unresolved.
The online application may only be submitted/certified by the chief school officer of the applicant LEA. The designated superintendent of an LEA is the only administrator with the submit/certify rights necessary to successfully submit and certify a completed application for NYSED review.
The FS-10 budget (Excel version preferred) should be completed in a manner that clearly identifies and aligns proposed expenses to planning activities. In addition, be sure to specify if activities are occurring at the district or school building level.
There is no carryover for these funds. All costs must be encumbered during the project period.
Submission Instructions
LEAs are REQUIRED to upload a signed PDF in the Business Portal and send a
blue ink
signed original and two hard copies of an FS-10 budget form to:
NYS Education Department - Office of Accountability
Attn: 2026 Title I, 1003 SIG (Planning)
89 Washington Avenue - Room 320 EB
Albany, NY 12234
Budget Amendment Deadline
The Field Support Services Unit requires the “
2025-26 Title I, 1003 School Improvement Grant (Amendment Request)
” survey be completed for electronic submission through the NYSED Business Portal. LEAs will need to answer four questions in the survey and upload a completed and signed PDF copy of their FS-10As.
All budget amendments should be discussed with the program office prior to the submission of an FS-10A. To ensure sufficient review and processing time, amendments to add new activities must be postmarked and submitted no later than June 1, 2026.
Questions
For additional information or assistance please contact:
fieldsupport@nysed.gov
.

Purpose
Pursuant to New York State Education Law
§2814
: Omnibus school violence prevention grant program, the primary purpose of the Extended School Day/School Violence Prevention (ESD/SVP) Program is to award competitive grants to provide support to students through extended school day activities and/or school safety programs that promote violence prevention. Programs must demonstrate consistency with the school safety plans required by
§2801-a
of New York State Education Law and should not displace existing school district after-school funding.
Under State Education Department bill S4598D, school-based and school-affiliated anti-gun and anti-violence programs are now eligible as school safety activities under this grant. Public school districts and not-for-profit organizations working in collaboration with a public school district(s) may submit an application to conduct either an ESD program or an SVP program.
Applicants may apply for both programs; however, a separate application is required for each.
Project Period
July 1, 2026 - June 30, 2031
Eligible Applicants
Public school districts and not-for-profit organizations working in partnership with one or more public school districts are eligible to apply.
Amount of Funding
Approximately $24.3 million is expected to be available annually. Funding beyond Year One will be contingent upon the State Legislature appropriating funds. Each application may include a request for an annual grant award of a maximum of $450,000. The Extended School Day (ESD) and School Violence Prevention (SVP) applications are separate, but an eligible entity may apply for both. If the entity applies for both, the total funding applied for may not exceed $450,000. For instance, if an entity is applying for $250,000 with ESD, it can only apply for $200,000 with SVP, for a total of $450,000. Eligible school districts cannot apply as an individual district and also apply as part of a consortium.
The minimum annual award for an Extended School Day grant will be $125,000. However, there is no minimum award amount established for a School Violence Prevention grant. Funds will be allocated to each geographic area as follows: 40% to New York City; 10% to the big four cities of Buffalo, Rochester, Syracuse, and Yonkers; and 50% to the Rest of the State, including at least 15% guaranteed to High Needs Rural applicants. If not enough High Needs Rural applications meet the scoring threshold outlined in the RFP, the portion of the guaranteed 15 percent not used would revert to the overall Rest of the State.
Prequalification Requirement
Proposals received from nonprofit applicants that are not Prequalified in the Statewide Financial System (SFS) by 5:00 PM on the proposal due date
April 17, 2026
, cannot be evaluated. Such proposals will be disqualified from further consideration. Please see the “Prequalification Requirement” section of the RFP for additional information.
Non-mandatory Notice of Intent
The Notice of Intent (NOI) is not a requirement for submitting a complete application by the application date; however, NYSED strongly encourages all prospective applicants to submit an NOI to ensure a timely and thorough review and rating process. A non-profit applicant’s NOI will also help to facilitate timely review of their prequalification materials. The notice of intent is a simple notification stating your organization’s (use the legal name) intent to submit an application for this grant. Please also include your organization’s NYS Vendor ID. The due date is April 3, 2026. Please send the NOI by email to
ESDSVPRFP@nysed.gov
.

RFP 237 –  Extended School Day / School Violence Prevention Grant  
Round 5 Q&A - Eligibility Questions  
• Are we allowed to submit multiple applications for different schools? E.g., an application for ESD at a 
middle school and a separate application for ESD to a different program at a high school. 
o Yes, however, the total amount that any district or non -profit applicant may apply for is $450,000.  
o Public school districts can either submit separate applications for individual schools or submit one 
application for multiple schools within the district, proposing appropriate programs for various grade 
levels, as long as those programs are aligned with the goals and objectives of the grant.    
o CBOs can either submit separate applications for individual schools or submit one application for 
multiple schools within the same district.  
• Can one application support multiple schools? I.e., could one application fund an after -school program at a 
middle school and a separate high school?  
o Yes, however, the total amount that any district or non -profit applicant may apply for is $450,000.  
o Public school districts can either submit separate applications for individual schools or submit one 
application for multiple schools within the district, proposing appropriate programs for various grade 
levels, as long as those programs are aligned with the goals and objectives of the grant.    
o CBOs can either submit separate applications for individual schools or submit one application for multiple schools within the same district.  
• How many applications is a non-profit corporation allowed to submit?   
o While there is no limit to the number of applications an eligible applicant can submit, the total amount 
that any district or non-profit applicant may apply for is $450,000.   
o ESD applicants should keep in mind that the minimum number of children to be served in any one application is 50, and the minimum award allocation is $125,000.  
• For the extended day school grant, can an organization submit more than one application? For example, let's say we have two schools we are partnering with.  Can we submit two separate applications?  
o Yes, you can submit two applications. There is no limit to the number of applications an eligible applicant 
can submit. However, the total amount that any applicant may apply for is $450,000.  
• What is the maximum number of applications that a non-profit organization can submit? Is it 1 for ESD 
and 1 for SVP?   
o There is no limit to the number of applications an eligible applicant can submit. However, if submitting 
multiple applications for ESD and/or SVP, the total combined amount that a nonprofit applicant or single 
district may apply for is $450,000.  
• Is an eligible entity (such as a not -for-profit organization) permitted to submit more than one SVP 
application if each proposal represents a distinct project or set of schools, or is there a limit of one SVP 
application per applicant?  If multiple applications are permitted, is there a maximum total amount an 
organization may request across all SVP applications?  
o There is no limit to the number of applications an eligible applicant can submit. However, if submitting 
multiple applications for SVP, the total combined amount that a nonprofit applicant or single district may 
apply for is $450,000.  

• We are planning to submit a proposal for Extended School Day. Is it acceptable to include schools from 
more than one NYC school District in the same ESD application? For example, we want to include one 
school from NYC District 7 and one school from District 9.  
o Yes, as a CBO applicant, it is acceptable to include schools from more than one school district in the 
same ESD application,  provided you have signed partnership agreements with each school and district.  
• If a non -profit organization can submit multiple applications, is there a funding amount limit for a single 
non-profit organization?   
o If submitting multiple applications for ESD and/or SVP, the total combined amount that a nonprofit 
applicant or single district may apply for is $450,000. However, a non-profit organization could apply for 
up to $450,000 as the lead applicant and also be a partner on applications submitted by a district or 
multiple districts. The $450,000 funding cap applies to applicants, not partners.  
• Can a not -for-profit apply for more than one ESD grant if each application will serve a different school 
district?  
o Yes, however,  if submitting multiple applications for ESD and/or SVP, the total combined amount that a 
nonprofit applicant or single district may apply for is $450,000.  
o In addition to applying for the maximum award of $450,000, a not -for-profit organization could also be a 
partner on more than one district application.  
o There is no limit to the number of school district  applicants  a not -for-profit can be in partnership with.  
• I have a question regarding page 3 of the RFP, which provides, in paragraph 4, "Each applicant must 
adhere to the cap on the number  of applications and total funding request  as outlined in the eligibility 
section." I don't see information about  the cap anywhere else in the RFP and there does not seem to be a 
defined eligibility section. The only  information  on eligibility seems to be on page 1, where eligible 
applicants are defined as "public school districts and not -for-profit organizations working  in partnership 
with  one or more public school districts are eligible to apply." There is no language about a cap on the 
number of applications in this section. Can you clarify this cap?  
o There is no limit to the number of applications an eligible applicant can submit. However, the total 
amount that any applicant may apply for is $450,000. A revised RFP has been posted with “cap on the 
number of applications” removed.  
• What is the "cap on the number of applications and total funding requested as outlined in the eligibility 
section"? There is no eligibility section in the RFP. I know that each application is limited to $450,000 but 
may a CBO submit more than one application?  
o There is no limit to the number of applications an eligible applicant can submit. However, the total 
amount that any applicant may apply for is $450,000.  
• Is an eligible entity (such as a not -for-profit organization) permitted to submit more than one SVP 
application if each proposal represents a distinct project or set of schools? Or is there a limit of one SVP 
application per applicant?  If multiple applications are permitted, is there a maximum total amount an 
organization may request across all SVP applications?  
o There is no limit to the number of SVP applications an eligible applicant can submit. However, the total 
amount that any applicant may apply for across all applications is $450,000.  
• Is $450,000 the maximum that one non -profit organization can apply for, regardless of the number of 
applications?  
o Yes 

o In addition to applying for the maximum award of $450,000, a not -for-profit organization could also be a 
partner on more than one district application.  
o There is no limit to the number of school district  applicant s a not -for-profit can be in partnership with.  
• We are looking to apply for individual ESD/SVP contracts at multiple schools. The previous RFP's limit 
was $1,200,000 per organization but $350,000 per application.  Is our agency restricted to this new $450,000 
funding limit for all applications at multiple sites, or is that limit per site with the ability to exceed it up to 
the $1,200,000 limit per organization? 
o The limit any one agency can apply for is $450,000.  
o However, an agency could apply for up to $450,000 as the lead agency  and also  be a partner 
organization on one or more school district applications.  
• Is a Community -Based Organization (CBO) permitted to submit two separate ESD applications for two 
different schools? If so, would the maximum award amount of $450,000 apply to each application, or would 
the organization need to split the $450,000 across both applications?  
o The maximum award amount that a CBO can apply for, across one or multiple applications, is $450,000.  
o However, an agency could apply for up to $450,000 as the lead agency and also be a partner organization on one or more school district applications.  
• Can a CBO apply for multiple grants with different school districts?  
o Yes, but the limit any one agency can apply for is $450,000.  
o However, an agency could apply for up to $450,000 as the lead agency  and also be a partner 
organization on one or more school district applications.  
• Can you please let us know what the total agency cap is on proposal submissions?   For example, our agency 
currently has 3 applications totaling $348,800 each.   Are we correct in that we can submit three new 
proposals each not exceeding   $450,000 each  
o No, that is not correct. The total combined amount that a nonprofit applicant may apply for is $450,000.   
• What is the maximum funding that a non-profit organization can be awarded for this RFP? Would it be $450,000?  
o The total that a non-profit organization or a single district may apply for is $450,000 per agency. Consortia applicants may apply for up to $1.2M, with no more than $450,000 allocated for any one 
district of the consortium.  
• Is there a designated amount of award funding allocated specifically for CBOs?  
o No, there is no designated amount of award funding allocated specifically for CBOs.  
• Can charter schools apply on their own?  
o Charter schools are not eligible to apply  
• We will be applying for our charter school, which has three schools. Can the 2 hours/day for three days be 2 hours for one day/week at each school or does it need to be 2 hours/3 days/week for each school? Does the 
240 total minimum hours need to be at each of the three schools or for the charter system as a whole?  
o Charter schools are not eligible to apply  
• Are Charter Schools eligible to apply?  
o Charter schools are not eligible to apply  

• For RFP 237, Omnibus School Violence Prevention Grant Program (Extended School Day and School 
Violence Prevention), can you please confirm whether a New York State charter school that functions as its 
own LEA is eligible to apply directly as a public school district applicant?  
o Charter schools are not eligible to apply  
• I am writing to seek clarification on school eligibility for RFP #237 Extended School Day / School Violence 
Prevention. On the RFP Appendix C, charter schools are classified as its own category under the Need 
Resource Capacity Index : 
• We are located in NYC and would like to include a Charter high school in our proposal, which would 
also include two NYC Department of Education high schools  
• Would a Charter school be considered as an NYC school within its respective geographic district?  
• Can we include one charter school and two NYC District  public schools on the same application?   
o Charter schools are not eligible to apply  
• I am a grant evaluator for ESD/SVP, and in sharing the new RFP with current and prospective applicants, 
can you please clarify if a CBO or LEA can apply if they have other OST grants such as 21st CCLC, 
LEAPS, BOOST, etc.?   
o Yes. There is nothing that would prohibit a CBO or LEA that has other OST grants from applying. However, ESD/SVP applicants shall be prohibited from using ESD/SVP funds to displace after -
school funding in existence (Education Law, Article 55, § 2814(1)). Each grant -funded program (i.e., 
21st CCLC, ESD/SVP) has unique guidelines and requirements. Following the expiration of a 
funding source in one grant award period, a new grant application may replace previous 
programming if the proposed program meets the requirements of the ESD/SVP program and is 
awarded funds.  
• Our district currently receives 21st Century Community Learning Center (21st CCLC) funding. Are we eligible to apply for RFP 237 to expand services at our current sites, or would this be considered a 
duplication of federal/state funding?  
o Yes. There is nothing that would prohibit a CBO or LEA that has other OST grants from applying. 
However, ESD/SVP applicants shall be prohibited from using ESD/SVP funds to displace after -
school funding in existence (Education Law, Article 55, § 2814(1)). Each grant -funded program (i.e., 
21st CCLC, ESD/SVP) has unique guidelines and requirements.  
• If a site is already receiving 21st CCLC funding, can we apply for RFP 237 to serve a different cohort of 
students (e.g., different grade levels or specific high -need groups) at that same location?  
o Yes 
• We are a small public school. We have only an extended school year summer program. Would we be 
eligible for these grant programs? Do we have to have a program in place already?   
o Yes. Public school districts are eligible for this grant. You do not need to currently have a program in place.  
• Can we apply for our community center program, which is offered to youth grades 9 -12? 
o Public school districts and not -for-profit organizations working in partnership with one or more 
public school districts are eligible to apply.  
• I recognize that there's a $450,000.00 limit per school.   Is there a limited number of schools we can partner 
with?   

o As a lead applicant, you’re limited to $450,000 in total funding applied for. There is no limit to the 
number of schools a CBO can partner with.  
• Is there a cap for organizations listed as partners or leads in multiple proposals? In the past an 
organization could only receive $1,200,000 across grants.  
o As a lead applicant, you’re limited to $450,000 in total funding applied for.  There is no limit to the 
number of schools a CBO can partner with.

Purpose of 
Grant  Pursuant to New York State Education Law §2814 : Omnibus school 
violence prevention grant program, the primary purpose of the Extended 
School Day/School Violence Prevention (ESD/SVP) Program is to award 
competitive grants to provide support to students through extended school day activities and/or school safety programs that promote violence prevention.  Programs must demonstrate consistency with the school safety 
plans required by §2801- a of New York State Education Law and should not 
displace existing school district after -school funding.  
 
Under State Education Department bill S4598D, school -based and school -
affiliated anti -gun and anti -violence programs are now eligible as school 
safety activities under this grant. Public school districts and not -for-profit 
organizations working in collabor ation with a public school district(s) may 
submit an application to conduct either an ESD program or an SVP program.  Applicants may apply for both programs; however, a separate 
application is required for each.

Application Guidance  
Description of Program  
The Extended School Day (ESD) and School Violence Prevention (SVP) applications are 
separate. An eligible entity may apply for both programs but must submit a separate application for each. If the entity applies for both, the total funding applied for may not exceed $450,000.  
The goal of the ESD program is to provide extracurricular enrichment activities that address the following domains: academic enrichment, social -emotional learning, arts and 
culture, physical health and wellness, community and civic engagement, and violence  
prevention, which  will contribute to increased student achievement and school violence 
prevention.  
The goal of the SVP program is to incorporate safety measures, such as secure corridors, diversity programs, collaboration with law enforcement and community organizations, and the use of safety technologies, including metal detectors, intercom systems, and other communication devices, to increase school security and the safety of school personnel and students by addressing the program’s prescribed objectives.  
Goods and services must be itemized in the budget narrative. Each applicant must adhere to the cap on total funding requested as outlined in the eligibility section.  
The target number of students for ESD programs is called the Target Participation Number, and for SVP programs is called the total students to be served.  
Extended School Day Model  
The maximum award for an individual Extended School Day (ESD) project will be $450,000 at a maximum allocation of $2,500 per student. The minimum award allocation will be $125,000. Applicants are expected to provide extracurricular enrichment activities, 
including, but not limited to, athletics, academic enrichment, social -emotional learning, 
art, music, drama, academic tutoring, mentoring, community services, and related programs that will increase student achievement and contribute to school violence prevention by addressing the program's prescribed objectives.  
In addition, the application must meet the following requirements:  
• Serve children within the range of grades Pre- K through 12.  
• Operate outside the regular school day; programs may operate before or after school, on weekends , and during school breaks . 
• Summer programming is allowable if provided in addition to extended school day programming during the academic year. Summer -only programming is not 
allowable . 
• Operate for a minimum of 6 program hours per week . 
• Operate for a minimum of 240 program hours per site p er program year . 
• Serve a minimum of 50 children.  

 
4 • Demonstrate that programming will start on or before November 1, 2026, except 
for NYSED -approved reasons . 
 
The number of students will be based on the “unduplicated count,” which is the number of unique participants from July 1 to June 30 of each program year. A student qualifies as a participant if they have 15 hours or more of program participation. The target number of student participants for the ESD model will be called the Target Participation Number.  
School Violence Prevention Model  
The maximum award for an individual SVP project is $450,000. SVP projects are not subject to the $2,500 per student funding limit. Applicants should aim to enhance school safety by implementing measures such as secure corridors, diversity programs, collabo ration with law enforcement and community organizations, and the use of safety 
technologies, including metal detectors, intercom systems, and other communication 
devices, to increase school security and the safety of school personnel and students by 
addres sing the program's prescribed objectives.  
In addition, the application must meet the following requirements:  
• Serve students in grades Pre- K through 12.  
• Operate during regular school hours.  
• Demonstrate that intended measures would impact all school and/or district 
students and staff.  
Funds may not be used to purchase, maintain, or modify facial recognition software or 
devices.  
Additional school safety measures include:  
• Evidence- based youth programs that support positive youth development, 
leadership, empowerment, and anti -violence and peace promotion initiatives.  
• A combination of evidence- based, emerging, and promising practices focused on 
trauma -informed care and healing services, individual survivor -centered support, 
and community mental health efforts aimed at promoting student well -being in 
response to gun viol ence.  
• Anti-gun violence education programs.  
• Culturally responsive and sustaining programs.  
• Initiatives aimed at systemic change by holistically addressing violence and 
promoting a positive school climate through partnerships with community -based 
organizations.  
• Evidence- based school -wide behavioral intervention programs designed to 
address and de- escalate violent incidents within the school or community, mediate 
conflicts, link victims to support services, and promote neighborhood peace.  
• Evidence- based programs promoting social media safety and responsible digital 
citizenship.  
• Any other activity designed to meet students' physical, social, emotional, mental health, and academic needs while enhancing school safety and climate.

Safety and Health Requirements 
School district applicants must adhere to New York State’s SAVE Act , including 
provisions related to staff fingerprinting. District -led programs located in school buildings 
must comply with district -wide School Safety Plans and individual building- level 
Emergency Response Plans as outlined in  Before and After School Safety Planning 
Guidance.  
All program staff of district -led programs operating in a school building must be trained in 
and familiar with the School Emergency Response Plan and its emergency procedures. 
If the proposed district -led program is located at a site other than a school building, a 
SACC registration is required and an Emergency Response Plan must be developed as per New York State’s SACC regulations (see below for more information), and program staff must be trained to follow its procedures prior to commencing programming at the site(s).
 
District -run programs operating in a school building (not SACC registered) must also 
comply with NYSED laws and regulations for schools concerning health, including but not limited to medication administration, and training requirements for unlicensed staf f to 
administer epinephrine auto- injectors and glucagon to students with orders for such.   
 
All applicants must address how students will travel safely to and from programming and their homes.

If the lead applicant is a community organization and proposes to serve seven or more children under the age of 13 beyond school hours, whether in a school building or other location, the applicant must obtain School -Age Child Care (SACC) registration in 
accordance with the New York State Office of Children and Family Services (OCFS) 
Regulations at 18 NYCRR Part 414.   
If the lead applicant is an LEA intending to provide services at a location other than the 
school building and proposes to serve seven or more children under the age of 13 beyond 
school hours, the applicant must provide proof of application for a School -Age Child Care 
(SACC) registration in accordance with New York State Office of Children and Family 
Services (OCFS) Regulations at 18 NYCRR Part 414 at the time of the grant application. Final SACC registration approval is not required at the time of ESD or S VP application; 
however, proof of SACC application is required. A SACC registration must be obtained prior to the start of program services. A program that has applied for a SACC registration may begin programming temporarily as a single activity program until the SACC 
registration is obtained. Applicants who are required to have a SACC registration must 
either upload a current SACC registration or OCFS confirmation of SACC application with their ESD or SVP application into Survey Monkey Apply . If awarded, a valid SACC 
registration must be submitted to NYSED before full program implementation can begin 

 
6 and must occur within 90 days of receiving an award notification.  Applicants who fail to

registration or provide their  registration application number , where indicated in SMA. 
Failure to provide this information will result in disqualification.  Applicants are urged

1 for SACC

Administrative Cost Cap  
Administrative costs can be direct or indirect. No more than 5% of the total annual award may be used for administrative costs. Examples of administrative expenses include, but are not limited to, the cost of a principal who is required to remain in the building during program hours, but who does not provide direct service to program participants; the cost of fiscal employees or other staff members whose role is strictly oversight of the program and its staff; the cost of an audit; and the cost of office supplies that are not utilized by program participants.  
Each application must include the position of Program Director. The Program Director’s 
salary will not be included in the 5% administrative cap. For the purposes of this grant, 
program space rental and school usage fees are also considered direct costs and are 
excluded from the 5% administrative cap.  
Direct Service Level Participation 
The NYSED Consortium Policy states that a lead agency cannot act as a flow -through for 
grant funds to pass to other recipients. NYSED has established a minimum level of direct 
service of 25% to be provided by the applicant. Direct services can include costs 
associated with the Program Director, teachers, activity leaders, rent for program space, and school usage fees, as well as the provision of specific activities for students and families . On the Composite Budget (Attachment 8), no portion of Purchased 
Services may be considered a direct service by the lead agency.  
Indirect Costs Cap  
Applicants may include indirect costs in the budget. Indirect costs are costs of activities 
that benefit more than one program or objective and, therefore, cannot be readily assigned to only one specific program or objective. Indirect costs are generally c lassified 

 
10 under functional categories, including general maintenance and operational expenses, 
general office and administrative expenses, general overhead expenses, and other allowable general expenses. Indirect cost rates are included in calculating the 5% administrative cap.  
• School districts must use the restricted indirect cost rates calculated by NYSED.  
• Not-for-profit organizations must prepare their budgets using an indirect cost rate 
of up to 2.7%. If notified that they have been selected to receive funding, they may apply for a higher indirect cost rate of up to 8 percent, bearing in mind the administrative cost cap , by completing and submitting an FS -87-R Form to the 
Department. Note that approval for a higher indirect cost rate must be required and approved each year.  
For more information about indirect costs, visit the Grants Finance website.  
Professional Development and Training Cost Cap  
Up to 5% of the total annual award may be used for professional development and training related directly to ESD or SVP programs. Costs related to professional development and training provided for the program staff must be included in the budget.  
Program Evaluation Cost Cap  
An independent local program evaluator is required and must agree to the evaluation 
requirements as outlined in this RFP . Up to 6% of the total annual award may be allocated 
for an independent program evaluation. For more information, visit the Grants Finance 
FAQ webpage.

Performance report s should demonstrate that substantial progress has been made toward

Student Participation Roster  
For ESD programs, a roster of student participants, including their names and the total hours

period. At a minimum, grantees are required to maintain an enrollment form and parental 

 
12 permission on file for each participant. To qualify as a participating student, attendance 
records must reflect at least 15 hours of participation during the program year. The grantee's budget will be proportionally reduced if the submitted roster is less than 95% of the Target Participation Number specified in the composite budget.  
Shortfalls in ESD Participation  
Starting in year two and continuing annually, ESD grant award recipients must submit a 
roster of students enrolled in the program through a secure NYSED website, along with their 
number of participation hours for the year, to NYSED by July 15. To qualify and be counted as a participant, a student must attend for 15 hours or more.   
ESD program attendance is expected to reflect the Target Participation Number indicated 
in the grant application. The Target Participation Number will not change throughout the life 
of the grant.  
The roster of students participating for 15 hours or more will be compared to the Target 
Participation Number. If the current roster  of participants is less than 95% of the Target 
Participation Number, the grantee’s budget will be proportionally reduced by the percentage of the shortfall in the current program year.  Budgets will then reset to the original amount in 
the following year.  
Shortfalls in ESD Program Hours 
ESD grant award recipients must provide evidence of delivering at least 240 hours of 
programming per site during the program year. Starting in Year Two and continuing 
semiannually, recipients must report the total number of ESD program hours delivered by 
the midpoint and end of each program year as part of the required Mid -Year and Annual 
Reports.  
Grant recipients who do not meet the 240 -hour requirement in a given program year will be  
provided support and subject to additional monitoring by the ESD/SVP Program Office 
during the following program year.  
Failure to meet the 240 -hour goal in any two program years within the five -year grant cycle 
may result in the suspension or termination of grant funding.

Self-Assessment and Independent Evaluation Requirements 
Self-Assessment: ESD and SVP grantees must use a research- based planning and self -
assessment tool. This tool should be used by representatives of all stakeholders involved in 
the program to self -assess their program’s quality improvement and planning efforts, which 
will help their sch ool violence prevention efforts achieve the desired outcomes.  
For ESD programs, the program Quality Self -Assessment (QSA) Tool, a research- based 
planning and self -assessment tool developed by the New York State Network for Youth 
Success  (NYSNYS), must be used by representatives of all stakeholders involved in the 
program to promote program quality. The Quality Self -Assessment (QSA) Tool , although 
not considered an evaluation tool, does provide an opportunity for feedback that will contribute to program improvement efforts leading to better program outcomes.  
Independent Evaluation: Grantees must contract with an independent evaluator to assess 
their progress in achieving the objectives of their ESD or SVP program, ensuring the delivery of high -quality after -school and school violence prevention initiatives and attainment of 
program outcomes. Their primary role is to develop an evaluation plan, analyze program data, identify key insights, and effectively communicate actionable findings and recommendations for improvement, as well as track the program's progress toward achieving its objectives. The cost of the independent evaluation must not exceed 6% of the grantee’s total annual budget. Additionally, the contracted independent evaluator cannot serve as the primary grant writer for the ESD or SVP application. It is 
understood, however, that the evaluator will be writing the evaluation plan.  
The independent evaluation must assess both program implementation and outcomes using a combination of quantitative and qualitative measures. Each program year must include two on- site visits (Fall and Spring) to provide direct observation and in -depth analysis of 
program implementation and effectiveness. The independent evaluation results must be used to refine, improve, and strengthen the program, and they must be made available to the ESD/SVP Program Office upon request.  
Implementation evaluation activities include assessing whether the program is being 
executed with fidelity to its original design. This entails, but is not limited to:  
• Collaboratively determining the readiness for program evaluation, including whether 
major program components are in place.  
• Document review of schedules and procedures in place and observation of program 
activities to assess whether all program components are being implemented with fidelity to the program as outlined in the grant application.  
• Making recommendations to support program enhancements, identify best practices, 
and adjust strategies for greater impact.  
Outcome evaluation activities measure the effect of program implementation on the 
intended recipients of services. The Activities, Measures, and Indicators of Success 

 
14 Template (Attachment 6A or 6B) outlines the activities and their intended outcomes. 
Intended outcomes include improving student achievement, preventing school violence, and 
enhancing school safety, as applicable. The evaluation framework should:  
• Specify how progress toward these goals will be assessed, utilizing qualitative and quantitative data.  
• Incorporate the ongoing use of a school climate survey to capture perceptions of 
safety, inclusivity, and the overall school environment, ensuring a comprehensive 
assessment of the program's impact.  
The measuring of program outcomes could be done without requiring student -level data 
(PII). Data could be collected anonymously, through such means as focus groups, surveys (self -report) and school climate measures. However, the proposed evaluation 
plan may include measuring program participants’ academic improvement, for example, which may require the analysis of student -level data using such measures as state 
assessment scores. If so, the independent evaluator would have to request the release of student -level data on program participants from the district. This would require the 
evaluator to have a data- sharing  agreement in place with the student’s school district. 
The district may not be willing to share student PII but may be willing to aggregate the student -level data and then share the required data in aggregate form.  Or the district 
may be willing to secur ely share the student -level data with the evaluator, with the 
appropriate security and confidentiality agreements in place. The evaluator would then report outcomes in aggregate form only, thereby protecting the students’ privacy.  
If the need for PII is included in your Evaluation Plan:  
If your proposed evaluation plan includes outcomes requiring student PII, be sure the 
evaluator and the district enter into a data- sharing agreement prior to submitting your 
grant application. District applicants must sign a data- sharing agreement with the 
evaluator if PII is needed. In addition to a signed data- sharing agreement between the 
district and evaluator, CBO applicants should also include the sharing of student data in 
its signed Partnership Agreement with the district. All CBO applicants are req uired to 
submit a Partnership Agreement with the district superintendent, principal(s) and CBO 
representative’s signatures, so that responsibilities of all parties are fully delineated.  
Key Deliverables Provided by the Independent Evaluator to the Program  
• Evaluation Plan with Logic Model/Theory of Change:  Updated annually to align 
with program goals and improvements.  
• Semi -Annual Evaluation Reports: Comprehensive assessments that track 
implementation and outcomes.  
• Findings and Recommendations : Concise, reader -friendly summaries of key 
insights from data analyses of the required semi -annual site visits.  
Program Monitoring 
Grantees operating an ESD or SVP program may be required to have their program 
monitored by NYSED to ensure compliance with state regulations and proper grant implementation. The ESD/SVP Program Office manages this oversight through on -site and 
desk monitoring reviews. A risk assessment will assist NYSED in identifying which grantees 

 
15 will be selected for monitoring each program year and in determining whether the review will 
be conducted on -site or through a desk -based monitoring process.  
The risk assessment considers:  
• Grantee compliance with the submission of timely reporting.   
• ESD/SVP Program Office concerns, including (but not limited to) fiscal, 
communication, and quality of program implementation .  
• Lack of progress in meeting required goals and objectives .  
Grantees participating in either site or desk monitoring will be notified in advance and must 
provide evidence of several indicators of success, including, but not limited to:  
• Administration/Organization for Programming .  
• Staffing/Professional Development .  
• Programming and Activities . 
If areas for improvement are identified during monitoring, the ESD/SVP Program Office will 
outline them in an Action Plan, set a deadline for demonstrating progress , and provide 
necessary support . All identified areas must be resolved or actively addressed to the 
satisfaction of NYSED.  
Failure to resolve or address identified areas may result in the suspension of funding.  
NYSED Consortium Policy for State and Federal Discretionary Grant 
Programs  
Participants can form a consortium to apply for the grant. To do so, the consortium must meet the following requirements:  
1. The consortium must designate one of the members to serve as the applicant and fiscal agent for the grant. The applicant agency must be an eligible grant recipient. All other consortium members must be eligible grant participants, as defined by the program  statute or regulation.  
2. In the event a grant is awarded to a consortium, the grant or grant contract will be prepared in the name of the applicant agency/fiscal agent, not the consortium, since the group is not a legal entity.  
3. The applicant agency/fiscal agent must meet the following requirements:  
A. Must be an eligible grant recipient as defined by statute.  
B. Must receive and administer the grant funds and submit the required reports to account for the use of grant funds.  
C. Must require consortium partners to sign an agreement with the fiscal agent that specifically outlines all services each partner agrees to provide.  
D. Must be an active member of the partnership/consortium.  
E. Cannot act as a flow -through for grant funds to pass to other recipients. NYSED 
has established a minimum level of direct service of 2 5% to be provided by the 
fiscal agent.

Purpose of Grant
To encourage the proper care and accessibility of research materials in the State, to promote the use and development of guidelines and standards for conservation/preservation work, and to support the growth of local and cooperative preservation programs. To provide modest financial support for projects that contribute to the preservation of significant research materials in libraries, archives, historical societies, and other agencies within the State of New York, whether by improving collection storage environments, reformatting or treating collections or other preservation activities described in these guidelines.
Grant Term
July 1st, 2026 - June 30th, 2027
Description of Program
The New York State Discretionary Grant Program for the Conservation and Preservation of Library Research Materials was authorized under Education Law, Section 273.6(c) in 1984, expanded in 1986 and revised in Part O, Chapter 57, of the Laws of 2005.  Its purpose is to encourage the proper care and accessibility of research materials in the State, to promote the use and development of guidelines and standards for conservation/preservation work, and to support the growth of local and cooperative preservation programs.
The Discretionary Grant Program provides modest financial support for projects that contribute to the preservation of significant research materials in libraries, archives, historical societies and other agencies within the State of New York, whether by improving collection storage environments, reformatting or treating collections or other preservation activities described in these guidelines.
Eligibility
Agencies and libraries chartered by the Regents, not-for-profit libraries, archives, historical societies, and similar agencies within the State, and from consortia or cooperating groups of such agencies. See the RFP documents Eligibility section for more details.
Amount of Funding
Source: New York State Aid to Libraries
Estimated Funds Available:
$500,000
Estimated Size of Awards: Minimum grant award is $2,500; maximum grant award is $45,000
Awards will be made subject to appropriation and availability of funds
Match Requirement: No financial match is required. See RFP document for Institutional Contribution of staff time requirements

Proposals received from nonprofit applicants that are not Prequalified in the Statewide Financial System (SFS) by
5:00 PM on the proposal due date of April 1st, 2026
